title: Batching + Concurrency Capacity Playbook
content:
Goal: produce a compact, actionable sizing and cost-model guide for continuous batching + concurrency tuning. For SRE/Serving and anyone feeding capacity numbers into Dedicated cost sheets. This is intentionally pragmatic: heuristics, spreadsheet column definitions, example calculations, and a short check-list for rollout.

Background/context
- Continuous batching (CB) dramatically reduces token cost by combining requests into larger GPU batches while keeping latency budgets via controlled queuing and concurrency limits.
- Two knobs: batch window (how long we allow requests to collect) and concurrency (how many in-flight batches / tokens we allow per model replica).
- Tradeoffs: higher batching -> lower cost/unit but increases p95 due to queueing; higher concurrency -> more throughput but increases instantaneous GPU memory pressure and tail latency variability.

Scope of this doc
- Small formula-driven model you can drop into a sheet for early sizing. Not a full simulator. Useful for: rough Dedicated pool sizing, expected token/sec, cost per 1M tokens, and p95 latency back-of-envelope.

Key assumptions (explicit)
- Single model, fixed generation length distribution (use mean and 95th token length).
- GPU peak throughput for token generation measured as tokens/sec when saturated at target batch size Bsat. We require a measured point: tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat.
- Batch build rate approximated by arrival rate lambda (requests/sec), and tokens-per-request distribution averaged to tokens_per_request.
- Queue discipline: FIFO within a small, bounded build window (w ms). Batches dispatched at either max batch size or after window expires.
- Concurrency defined as number of simultaneous batches being executed per replica (c).
- Ignore complex KV cache eviction dynamics; assume KV hits for prefix reuse reduce effective tokens generated by factor k_cache_hit_rate.

Spreadsheet layout / column definitions (drop into sheet columns left-to-right)
- A: scenario_name (string)
- B: requests_per_sec_lambda (numeric) -- observed/target steady arrival rate
- C: avg_tokens_per_request (numeric) -- e.g., 40
- D: p95_tokens_per_request (numeric) -- e.g., 120
- E: batch_window_ms (numeric) -- w, e.g., 50ms
- F: max_batch_size (numeric) -- hardware/software cap, e.g., 128
- G: tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat (numeric) -- measured from perf test, e.g., 16000 tokens/sec at Bsat=64
- H: target_p95_latency_ms (numeric) -- e.g., 300ms
- I: effective_arrival_rate_tokens_per_sec = B*C * (1 - k_cache_hit_rate) -- formula text: =B*C*(1 - cache_factor)
- J: expected_batch_fill = min(F, ceil( (B*(w/1000)) )) -- approximate avg requests per window
- K: avg_tokens_per_batch = J * C
- L: batch_generation_time_ms = (avg_tokens_per_batch / tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat) * 1000 * (Bsat_adjust_factor)
   - note: Bsat_adjust_factor accounts for sublinear perf vs batch: if avg batch smaller than Bsat, we approximate tokens/sec scales linearly; if larger, cap at measured Bsat perf. For simplicity use: tokens_per_sec_eff = tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat * (avg_batch_size / Bsat)
- M: queue_wait_ms = max(0, ( (J - 1) / B ) * 1000 * (w / max(1,J)) ) -- simple estimate; more simply: queue_wait ≈ w/2 if using fixed window dispatch
- N: p95_latency_ms_estimate = queue_wait_ms + batch_generation_time_ms + network_overhead_ms
- O: concurrency_per_replica = c (input)
- P: tokens_in_flight_per_replica = concurrency_per_replica * avg_tokens_per_batch
- Q: replica_capacity_tokens_per_sec = tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat * (concurrency_per_replica) * (efficiency_factor)
- R: replicas_needed = ceil( I / Q )
- S: cost_per_replica_per_hour = input from pricing sheet
- T: hourly_cost = R * S
- U: cost_per_1M_tokens = (hourly_cost / (I * 3600)) * 1e6

Important formula notes / heuristics
- Approximate queueing: For small windows (<100ms) and Poisson arrivals, avg wait ≈ w/2 but p95 wait ≈ w (worst-case) if window-based dispatch. Use p95_wait = min(w, 2*(w/2) + jitter_factor). Be conservative.
- If arrival rate is low relative to 1/w, most batches will be 1 request -> batching gains minimal. Add a flag in sheet: batching_effective_flag = J>1.
- Concurrency sizing rule of thumb (start here): c = max(1, floor( target_throughput_tokens_per_sec_per_replica / (avg_tokens_per_batch / batch_generation_latency_sec) )) but practically start at c=2..4 for LLMs with KV memory.
- GPU memory headroom: tokens_in_flight matters for KV caching and peak memory. Estimate mem_per_token * tokens_in_flight + base_model_mem < gpu_mem * 0.85. Put mem_per_token as tuning variable.

Worked example (numbers for sanity check)
- lambda = 60 req/s, avg_tokens = 40, p95_tokens = 130, w=40ms, F=64, tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat=16000 at Bsat=64, cache_hit_rate=0.15, network_overhead=20ms, efficiency_factor=0.9, concurrency=3, cost_per_replica_per_hour=7.20
- I = 60 * 40 * (1 - 0.15) = 2040 tokens/s
- J = min(64, ceil(60 * 0.04)) = ceil(2.4)=3 requests per batch on average
- avg_tokens_per_batch = 3 * 40 = 120 tokens
- batch_generation_time = (120 / 16000) * 1000 = 7.5ms (we'll multiply by 1 since Bsats match)
- queue_wait ~ w/2 = 20ms (p95_use w=40ms conservatively) -> p95_wait = 40ms
- p95_latency_estimate = 40 + 7.5 + 20 = 67.5ms -> under 300 target easily
- tokens_in_flight_per_replica = 3 * 120 = 360 tokens in flight
- replica_capacity_tokens_per_sec = 16000 * 3 * 0.9 = 43200 tokens/s (note: this is optimistic; bounded by other factors; we recommend sanity cap at tokens_per_sec_at_Bsat * 10 for multi-concurrency)
- replicas_needed = ceil(2040 / 43200) = 1 replica (ok in this toy example)
- hourly_cost = 1 * 7.2 = $7.2 -> cost_per_1M_tokens = (7.2 / (2040*3600)) * 1e6 ≈ $0.98 per 1M tokens

When this model breaks (red flags)
- arrival bursts with high variance (CV>2) will greatly increase p95 latency; consider moving to dynamic small windows + adaptive dispatch.
- if p95_tokens >> avg_tokens, concurrency that is safe at average can blow up memory at tails. Use p95_token column to check worst-case tokens_in_flight and add protective caps.
- if observed p95 latency >> estimate, instrument: batch sizes, batch build times, queue lengths, and per-request timing. Add tracing hooks (span: batch.build, batch.dispatch, batch.kv.load).

Practical tuning checklist (runbook)
- Step 0: Acquire perf numbers: tokens_per_sec at a measured batch size (Bsat) and memory footprint at that batch size. Add to pricing spreadsheet.
- Step 1: Populate arrival stats (lambda, avg, p95 token length) from production traces (sample 1% if necessary).
- Step 2: Run the spreadsheet above for multiple w candidates (20, 40, 80, 200 ms) and c candidates (1,2,3,4). Compare p95 and cost_per_1M_tokens.
- Step 3: Choose conservative config where p95_estimate <= target_p95 * 0.9 and replicas_needed has <20% headroom.
- Step 4: Canary: deploy with very small traffic (1–5% of traffic) and collect actual batch sizes, queue times, tail latencies.
- Step 5: If canary p95 > estimate by >30%, revert and choose smaller window or lower concurrency.

Open questions / TODOs for follow-up
- Replace window-based queueing estimate with simple M/D/1 or G/G/1 simulator in a python notebook; embed results in sheet snapshots.
- Add explicit KV cache model: per-prefix hit distribution impact on avg tokens generated per request.
- Cost model: align cost_per_replica with Dedicated pricing tiers and preemption risk modeling.
- Add per-region latency/network overhead baselines.

Notes to self / shorthand
- Keep spreadsheet lightweight: business users want a single numbers page (replicas_needed, cost per 1M tokens, p95_est). Keep detailed inputs on a hidden tab.
- Talk to Lina for memory-per-token numbers (LIN-ops TODO).
- Link perf run PR for tokens/sec at varying batch sizes: GH PR above.

References
- Internal perf runs: gh:raw/perf/2024-08-batching.csv referenced in PR 982
- Confluence draft for adaptive windows: page id in linked_artifacts

If you'd like I can dump a CSV-ready block for direct paste into a sheet (scenarios + header row) or a simple Python notebook that samples arrival distributions and simulates the fixed-window dispatcher. Say which you prefer.
